control_description: ICT Risk Profile, ICT Threat Landscape and Risk Categories
control_requirement: The ICT Threat Landscape must be maintained and regularly updated, include industry standard and knowledge bases, and shared with relevant stakeholders. The ICT Threat Landscape also must provide a risk-based view, which then motivates content and prioritization of ICT Control Framework and ICT Key Controls, respectively.

control_description: ICT Risk Profile, ICT Threat Landscape and Risk Categories
control_requirement: ICT threats must be monitored and classified with a rating of high significance where all of the following conditions are met: The threat, if occurred, could affect or could have affected critical or important functions of DBAG or related legal entities (including third-party providers, clients, or financial counterparts) based on available information. The threat has a high probability of occurrence at DBAG or related legal entities and must take into account at least the following elements: The capabilities and intent of threat actors to the extent known by DBAG or related legal entities. The persistence of the threat and any accrued knowledge about ICT-related incidents that have impacted DBAG or related legal entities or its third-party provider, clients, or financial counterparts. The geographical spread of the areas at risk ●

control_description: ICT Risk Profile, ICT Threat Landscape and Risk Categories
control_requirement: Insights from digital resilience testing, real-life ICT-related incidents (particularly cyber-attacks), challenges in executing ICT continuity and recovery plans, and information shared with counterparts during reviews must be consistently integrated in the ICT Threat Landscape and ICT Risk Categories.

control_description: ICT Risk Profile, ICT Threat Landscape and Risk Categories
control_requirement: ICT Risk Categories with a scenario description must be defined, refined, and operationalized based on the ICT Threat Landscape.

control_description: ICT Risk Profile, ICT Threat Landscape and Risk Categories
control_requirement: ICT Risk Categories must be mapped to an ICT Threat Landscape and include information of related control requirements as well as Primary and Secondary Assets with a focus on those supporting critical or important functions (CIF).

control_description: ICT Risk Profile, ICT Threat Landscape and Risk Categories
control_requirement: Relevant changes to the ICT Risk Profile must be monitored and reported to the ICT Risk Management Methodology owner while significant changes must be reported to the Management Body of DBAG and the legal entity, including the LE CISOs.
It must be ensured that the ICT Risk Assessment with ICT Risk Identification, Analysis and Evaluation is performed with sufficient resources, clearly defined responsibilities, and relevant risk data.
Associated roles and responsibilities for the ICT Risk Assessment must be defined.
ICT risk assessment must be performed on all legacy ICT Systems at least annually and additionally before and after connecting them to new IT Assets to ensure no new risks are introduced.

The ICT risk assessments of the affected Primary and Secondary Assets including the ICT risk treatment measures, if implemented, must be re-performed at least annually and in any of the following cases: Increase of the asset’s criticality New or stricter control requirement associated with the asset in the ICT Risk Guidelines Significant change with a security impact In case of special requests by third party or regulator Before the go-live Major change in the network and information system infrastructure, in the processes or procedures affecting their ICT supported business functions, information assets or ICT system assets ●
It must be ensured that ICT risks relevant to the organization are properly identified.
An ICT risk identification process must be established to identify potential ICT risks.

The identification of internal and external vulnerabilities and threats, particularly exposure to and from other financial entities, related to all relevant ICT supported business functions, Primary, and Secondary Assets must be conducted continuously. Risks (including linkage to ICT Threats) related to all relevant ICT supported business functions, Primary, and Secondary Assets must be at least annually. Monitoring of changes that could affect the ICT risk profile must enable their prompt detection. ●
It must be ensured that all identified ICT risks are analyzed.
An ICT risk analysis process must be in place to determine and analyze identified ICT risks based on their likelihood of occurrence and their potential impact.

The impact on DBAG or legal entities that might result from identified control requirement deviations considering the impact on loss of confidentiality, integrity, availability or authenticity of the assets and business impact such as financial, reputational, compliance impact or privacy violation must be assessed.
The likelihood of exploitation of identified control requirement deviations considering threats and vulnerabilities must be assessed.
As a result of the ICT risk analysis process, the ICT risk level based on impact and likelihood must be determined.
Qualitative and quantitative indicators to measure impact and likelihood of OpRisk scenarios based on ICT Threat Events, Risks, and vulnerabilities must be developed.
It must be ensured that identified ICT risks are evaluated, analyzed and prioritized.
An ICT Risk Evaluation process must be in place to evaluate the analyzed ICT risks resulting in a respective ICT risk level.
The risk must be determined and evaluated for all control requirement deviations considering impact and likelihood. The ICT risk level may take values: Very low (R1), Low (R2), Medium (R3), High (R4)
The ICT risks must be (re)evaluated in annual cycles, including a review of the effectiveness of implemented ICT risk treatment measures.
The ICT Risk Evaluation process must consider the ICT Risk Categories to categorize the resulting ICT Risk.
If the implemented ICT risk treatment measures prove to be ineffective, further ICT risk treatment must be performed.
It must be ensured that ICT risks are adequately treated.
An ICT risk treatment process must be in place to manage and respond to identified ICT risks.
ICT risk treatment plans must be created, documented, and maintained.
The ICT risk treatment plans must be signed off for all identified ICT risks by the respective Information Owner.

The ICT risk treatment plan must include, at a minimum, the following information: Selected treatment option including actions for implementation Rationale for the selection of the treatment options, including the expected benefits to be attained Responsible and accountable stakeholder for approving the treatment plan and implementing the plan
Information Owners should be prepared to demonstrate and provide updates on the status of implementation of the ICT risk treatment plan when required.

All identified ICT risks must be assigned to one of the following treatment options as part of the ICT risk treatment plan: “Accept” – acceptance of risk without mitigation (risks in scope for KRITIS assets must not be accepted if state-of-the-art mitigating measures are available and their use is appropriate). Risk acceptance is only possible for the remaining residual risk. “Mitigate” – implementation of mitigating measures to reduce the ICT risk level. “Avoid” – elimination of activities and exposures that can negatively affect Primary and Secondary Assets of the legal entities.

Selecting ICT risk treatment options must be based on clearly defined criteria which align with the organization’s risk appetite (specified in underlying Procedure documentation). To set criteria, the following should be considered: The nature and type of uncertainties that can affect outcomes and objectives (both tangible and intangible) How consequences and likelihood will be defined, predicted, and measured Time-related factors Consistency in the use of measurements How the level of risk will be determined How combinations and sequences of multiple risks will be taken into account The organization’s capacity
The decision for ICT risk acceptance must be based on the defined risk acceptance criteria.

Mitigating measures to reduce the ICT risks must be implemented in accordance with a defined ICT risk treatment plan. The risk mitigation timeline starts as soon as the risk has been assessed by the asset owner and timelines are defined as follows: High (R4): 3 months Medium (R3): 6 months Low (R2): 12 months Very low (R1): 18 months

Information Owner may decide on different timelines (shortened / extended) in case a proper justification is available and documented. In any case, the ICT risks must be (re)evaluated in annual cycles (please refer to 14.3).

The identified risks, related decisions, and information as well as the mitigating measures of the treatment plan, measure owners, agreed due dates and other related information such as the status from monitoring the ICT risk treatment plan must be documented in the risk registries.
After performing the ICT risk treatment, it must be assessed whether the risk tolerance levels of DBAG or the respective legal entity have been attained.

In case the defined risk tolerance levels cannot be attained through the implemented measures, the risk treatment plan must be revised and corrective actions to improve the ICT risk treatment measures must be documented.
It must be ensured that residual ICT risks that remain after the ICT risk treatment has been performed are handled appropriately.
A process to identify and determine residual ICT risks must be in place.

It must be ensured that residual ICT risks (e.g., in cases of risk acceptance) are identified and registered in an inventory, along with an acknowledgment of the residual ICT risk and an explanation for their acknowledgement.

Acknowledged residual ICT risks must be reviewed at least annually including: Identification of changes to residual risks Assessment of existing mitigation measures Assess if the reasons for accepting the residual risks are still valid

If the residual risks have changed, the implemented mitigation measures are no longer sufficient, or the reasons for accepting the residual risks are no longer valid, causing the residual risks to exceed the defined risk tolerance levels, a new ICT risk treatment must be performed.
Decisions on the acceptance and the review of residual ICT risks must be performed by Information Owners. ●
It must be ensured that ICT risks and related information are adequately communicated to the relevant stakeholders such as the Management Body.
The reporting to relevant stakeholders and decision makers (incl. Management Body) must take place with an aggregation appropriate to their roles and responsibilities related to ICT Risk management.

ICT risks identified as part of, and the results of ICT risk assessments, including the status of the ICT risk treatment plans must be communicated to the relevant stakeholders and decision makers up to the Management Body for review.

Identified ICT risks and relevant key indicators (e.g. risk appetite and tolerance levels, digital operational resilience metrics, etc.) must be reported regularly to: Appropriate stakeholders, including the ICT Risk Oversight and ICT Operational Management at least quarterly, at least monthly in case of R3 risks and immediately in case of identification of R4 risks The affected Management Body and LE CISOs at least quarterly and within a month in case of identification of R4 risks
All ICT risks must be registered in inventories which must be updated continuously and establish a monitoring and review process for continuous assessment and treatment of risks.
ICT risks with the highest ICT risk level must be assigned top priority and monitored closely with regular reporting on the actions that have been taken to mitigate them.
The fulfillment of ICT Risk control requirements must be documented for all Primary and Secondary Assets via ICT Risk documentation (e.g., ICT Risk, Security Documentation (SD) or similar).

Senior ICT staff must report at least yearly to the management body and LE CISOs on the following observations: ● - digital operational resilience testing, - real life ICT-related incidents, - cyber-attacks, - challenges faced upon the activation of ICT business continuity plans, and - challenges faced upon the ICT response and recovery plans.

control_description: Independent ICT Internal Controls Monitoring and Risk Assurance
control_requirement: It must be ensured that internal controls are monitored, ICT risk assurance is provided, and control effectiveness validated and reported to appropriate stakeholders such as Information and Asset Owners, executive boards of the legal entities.

control_description: Independent ICT Internal Controls Monitoring and Risk Assurance
control_requirement: Established and implemented ICT internal controls must be continuously monitored and validated to ensure that these controls are valid and effective.

control_description: Independent ICT Internal Controls Monitoring and Risk Assurance
control_requirement: Observations on the effectiveness of controls must be reported to control owners.
It must be ensured that lessons learned on the activities performed as part of an ICT Risk Management processes are captured and continuously used for improvement.

It must be ensured that the ICT Risk Management processes (incl. tool definitions, etc.) are reviewed and improved to be up to date with latest best practices and tailored to the needs of DBAG or the respective legal entity.
Independent reviews of ICT Risk Management processes and the implementation thereof must be performed and if necessary, corrective actions should be initiated.
Where appropriate, the results of monitoring technological developments must be used to update ICT Risk Management processes (incl. tools) and effectively combat ICT risk (e.g. cyberattacks).
A follow-up process and rules for the timely verification and remediation of critical ICT-related audit findings must be established.
The results of monitoring ICT Internal controls and the effectiveness of implemented ICT risk treatment measures must be used to correct and improve those measures.
ICT Risk management tools must be regularly reviewed and updated accordingly with the improvements to ICT Risk Management and related procedures and processes.
The ICT-related Operational Risk Scenarios must be reviewed on a regular basis, at least annually.

control_description: Provisions on Telecommunication Network and Services
control_requirement: It must be ensured that provisions for the telecommunication network and services, including relevant registration and responsibilities, are properly managed.

control_description: Provisions on Telecommunication Network and Services
control_requirement: A security officer must officially be nominated and contact details provided to the Bundesnetzagentur.

control_description: Provisions on Telecommunication Network and Services
control_requirement: The telecommunication network and telecommunication services must be registered at the Bundesnetzagentur.

It must be ensured that a sound and comprehensive Digital Operational Resilience Testing (DORT) Programme is established, maintained, and reviewed as an integral part of the ICT Risk Management Framework.
A DORT Programme must be established, documented, and maintained within the ICT Risk Management Framework.

The DORT Programme determine a suitable set of tests in a risk-based approach, such as vulnerability assessments and scans, open source analyses, network security assessments, gap analyses, physical security reviews, questionnaires and scanning software solutions, source code reviews where feasible, scenario-based tests, compatibility testing, performance testing, end-to-end testing, penetration testing, and threat-led penetration testing (TLPT).

The DORT Programme must follow a risk-based approach, taking into account: the evolving ICT risk landscape and ICT Threat Landscape as defined in ID 10, the proportionality principle with regard to the size and overall risk profile of the legal entity, the criticality of information assets and services provided, and the involvement of ICT third-party service providers.

The DORT Programme must define, for each testing type covered under 21.2: the applicable scope and asset coverage, the minimum frequency of execution, the methodology and approach to be applied, the independence requirements for testers, and the owning guideline or procedure containing the detailed technical specifications, if not already determined by the test owners.
The DORT Programme must define a programme lifecycle comprising:
Establish: Formal creation of the programme with defined scope, governance structure, resource allocation, and management body approval.

Maintain: Ongoing monitoring of programme execution, coverage tracking against the full test type inventory, and integration of new or changed testing requirements arising from changes to the ICT Threat Landscape, regulatory requirements, or the DOR strategy.

Review: Formal annual review of the programme's completeness, effectiveness, and alignment with DORA Art. 24(1), triggered additionally by: occurrence of a major ICT-related incident, supervisory instructions or findings, material changes to the legal entity's ICT environment or critical or important functions, and major risks from TLPT exercises.

Roles and responsibilities for the DORT Programme must be clearly defined and documented, including: The LE must designate a DORT Programme owner at appropriate seniority level responsible for programme governance, coordination across owning guidelines, and reporting to the management body. A clear allocation of responsibility for each testing type to the relevant guideline, procedure and operational responsibility for the execution of tests.

The DORT Programme must establish a centralized programme register that: Inventories all testing types with their defined scope, frequency, methodology reference, and owning guideline. Tracks the execution status of all planned tests against the programme schedule, including completion dates, responsible parties, and any deviations from planned frequencies. Records all findings identified across all testing types, their severity classification, remediation status, and linkage to the ICT risk register maintained under ID 17.4.

The results of all testing activities conducted under the DORT Programme must be integrated into the ICT Risk Management processes as follows: Testing findings must be forwarded continuously into the ICT risk identification and assessment processes defined in ID 12 and ID 13, and must inform updates to the ICT Threat Landscape maintained under ID 10.8. Testing findings that identify control deficiencies must trigger ICT risk treatment actions in accordance with ID 15, with remediation timelines aligned to the risk level determined under ID 14. Lessons learned from testing activities, including TLPT exercises, real-life ICT-related incidents, and challenges in executing ICT continuity and recovery plans, must be incorporated into the DORT Programme review process defined in 21.5.3 and into the DOR strategy maintained under ID 2.

DORT programme must report annually to the management body and LE CISOs covering as a minimum: The overall execution status of the programme against the planned schedule, including any deviations and their justification. A summary of findings identified across all testing types, their severity distribution, and the status of remediation actions. An assessment of the effectiveness of the programme in identifying weaknesses in the legal entity's digital operational resilience. Planned changes to the programme for the upcoming period, including any new testing types, scope expansions, or methodology updates.

The DORT Programme must ensure non-duplication and consistency across the framework by: Maintaining a clear mapping between each testing type and the single owning guideline or procedure containing its detailed technical specifications and execution requirements, avoiding conflicting requirements across guidelines Establishing a coordination mechanism between the DORT Programme owner and the operational owners of all referenced guidelines to ensure alignment upon any changes to testing requirements, frequencies, or methodologies.

control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: Security measures for IDP and Extended NCLC applications must be in place and commensurate with their classification, including documentation, access control, test management, business continuity management, periodic review, and transfer to regular applications.

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: The classification of information must determine the protection requirements for IDP and Extended NCLC applications (180 days) ●

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: If the protection requirements derived from the criticality exceed the technical protection possibilities of the IDP application (e.g., VBA password, file open password), appropriate protective measures must be taken.

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: To reduce risks regarding authenticity, integrity, or availability, IDP applications classified as critical and Extended NCLC applications classified as critical regarding confidentiality, authenticity, integrity or availability must be transferred into a regular application within three years after classification. A decommission plan for the specific replacement must be provided after one year (180 days) ●

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: Protection controls for IDP and Extended NCLC applications must follow a risk-based approach, thus demanding more strict control requirements for major and critical IDP and Extended NCLC applications classified as major/critical regarding confidentiality, authenticity, integrity or availability (180 days) ●

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: For minor and negligible IDP with high technical complexity and Extended NCLC applications classified as minor/negligible regarding confidentiality, authenticity, integrity or availability but high technical complexity, test management and access management must be in place (180 days) ●

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: For all major and critical IDPs and Extended NCLC applications classified as major/critical regarding confidentiality, authenticity, integrity or availability, processes must be established for appropriately allocating access rights to ensure that staff have only those rights that they need to perform their tasks. This includes the recertification process for authorizations (180 days) ●

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: All major and critical IDPs and Extended NCLC applications classified as major/critical regarding confidentiality, authenticity, integrity or availability must be secured against changes to the program logic in production (180 days) ●

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: For major and critical IDP with low technical complexity and Extended NCLC applications classified as major/critical regarding confidentiality, authenticity, integrity or availability but a low technical complexity a, test management and access management must be in place (180 days) ●

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: For major and critical IDP with low technical complexity and Extended NCLC applications classified as major/critical regarding confidentiality, authenticity, integrity or availability but a low technical complexity a, test management and access management must be in place (180 days) ●

control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: The availability of all IDP and Extended NCLC applications must at least be ensured by appropriate recovery mechanisms of the underlying file storage (180 days) ●

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: Authorized access to all IDP and Extended NCLC applications must at least be ensured by basic access control mechanisms (180 days) ●

control_description: Technical security measures for IDP and Extended No-/Low-Code Applications
control_requirement: For IDP with high technical complexity, measures and controls must be established to ensure the segregation of environments, the protection of data processed in non-production environments, the use of anonymized, pseudonymized or randomized data for testing, and the controlled, documented and approved use of production data where exceptionally required (180 days) ●

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_requirement: No‑/Low-code Applications must be governed using a proportional, risk‑based approach whereby all components (apps, flows, and environments) comply with ICT Risk Framework and are subject to control requirements commensurate with their business impact and technical complexity.

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance

control_requirement: Extended NCLC applications must apply enhanced governance by additionally ensuring that the inventory contains required information as defined in requirement ID 2.2, 2.3, adhering to lifecycle requirements defined in Requirement ID 2.8), implement segregated environment controls (Development / Test / Production) and protect the integrity and confidentiality of data in non-production environments, including the use of anonymized or pseudonymized data, and complying with applicable requirements mentioned in requirement ID 3, 4, 5, 7 where required based on criticality and technical complexity (180 days) ●

guideline_key: individual data processing no low code application governance
control_requirement: Advanced NCLC applications must be governed as regular IT Applications, complying with the applicable set of requirements applicable to regular IT applications, including formal governance, security, and SDLC controls (180 days) ●
For Identity and Access Management, procedures and controls must be defined, implemented, and performed.

A formal access management process, which includes the review and authorization of access requests by responsible authorities prior to provisioning, must be established, documented, and applied for all accounts and access rights.

Access requests and access provisioning for primary and secondary access must be documented accordingly. A central record must be available, preferably via a designated IAM tool, and allow the tracking of individual requests by MyUserID.
Access requests must be reviewed and authorized by responsible authorities or persons. An additional approval by the Role Owner is required for business-critical access.
Automated access provisioning must be established. If not possible, complementary controls must be designed, implemented, and described in the Authorization Concept.
An identity lifecycle process is established and must manage the creation, change, review and update, temporary deactivation, and termination of all accounts.

Entitlements in affected target ICT Systems and validation of entitlement creation by reconciliation between target ICT System and requested access must be enforced daily (including automated synchronization and clean-up of identified deviations). If not possible, complementary controls must be designed, implemented, and described in the Authorization Concept.
Applications should automatically be reconciled. If automatic reconciliation is not possible, complementary controls must be designed and implemented.
Access Rights for Identity Access Management must be defined and documented.
Access rights including remote and emergency access must be assigned and provisioned for IT Assets based on need-to-know, need-to-use and least privilege principles.
Access rights must be designed in alignment with the information classification of the information asset.

It must be ensured that roles and responsibilities are assigned to grant, review, and revoke access rights. Retention periods for logs must be defined in accordance with business and information security objectives, reason for event recording and results of the ICT risk assessment.
Role composition must be documented at the level of entitlements in a central tool.
Changes to the role composition must be processed (i.e. documented, approved, and tested) based on the change management process required in the Software and Change Management Guideline.
Segregation of Duties (SoD) must be defined, applied, and controlled to prevent any unauthorized access to sensitive data, circumventing access controls or conflicting business interests.

The Business Owner is responsible to assign all roles and entitlements to SoD areas for which Segregation of Duty is required and must be implemented at technical level. Roles assigned to SoD areas must be documented (e.g. in the Authorization Concept of the IT Asset).
SoD lifecycle change process must be documented.
Entitlements compositions must not contain any SoD conflict in itself.
Confirmed toxic SoD combinations must not be (re-) approved (ID 15 for further details).
Entitlements compositions must be assessed with respect to SoD requirements to enable SoD checks based on defined rules.
SoD must be reflected in the role composition.
The IT access rights allocated to staff must not conflict with any SoD defined rules.
While requesting and before assigning access to an account, SoD check and handling must be performed.
SoD conflicts must be classified and handled according to the defined and implemented SoD processes.
For each IT Asset an authorization concept must be developed, implemented, and kept up to date to prevent any unauthorized access or breach of access controls.
An Authorization Concept must cover at least the following scope items:
The Authorization Concept must be established based on the security requirements, business needs and the corresponding processes.
The Authorization Concept must define the complete design and content of roles and entitlements.
The Authorization Concept must define the design and management of user authorization and access (de-) provisioning.
The Authorization Concept must describe how emergency access is managed and controlled.
The Authorization Concept for the network infrastructure must define and describe the network access controls.
Authorization Concepts must be reviewed at least every 12 months and updated in case of changes.
Authorization Concepts must be approved prior to activating access rights.
The Information Owner of the adopting LE using the application must review the Authorization Concept.

Access controls must be defined, implemented, monitored and controlled to prevent any unauthorized access, avoid breach of access controls and restrict access to support the protection requirements considering each level of classification.
Unauthorized access must be defined, identified, prevented and denied by controls and measures for IT Assets and Non-IT Assets.

Entitlements for access to different Segregation Areas must only be assigned to users reflecting SoDs to access different Segregation Areas. Where separation of environment or duties is difficult (activities in the Green and Red Segregation Areas development and production activities performed by same teams), other controls such as monitoring of activities, audit trails and management supervision must be implemented.
User accounts should be clearly distinguishable in context of the user interface.

At least all accesses to Red and Yellow Segregation Area must be logged and all ICT Systems and users must only have access to networks and network services that they have been specifically authorized to use based on the need-to-know principle.

Controls must be designed and implemented to limit physical or logical access to Information Assets, IT Assets and Non-IT Assets fulfilling this Guideline which refers to access rights and access rights administration.

Controls and measures must be designed, implemented and managed to ensure that access to information and IT Assets are conducted using a unique identity. The established IAM lifecycle process must manage and control these unique identities.

All internal and external individuals, who have access to Information Assets and IT Assets, must have a unique, global user ID ("MyUserID") linked to a unique account. These accounts (other than shared accounts) must be linked to a MyUserID to remain traceable.

Information on the creation, modification or deletion of unique identifiers assigned to unique user accounts must be logged, monitored, maintained and kept for at least 18 month – even following a reorganization or end of a contractual relationship with the user.
Contractual obligations must consider the organisations demand on information security to ensure adherence and to prevent information leakage.

Personal secret authentication information such as passwords, PINs, keys, and tokens must never be shared or be made accessible to any other individual. The correct handling of cryptographic products and key material must be ensured and documented, and employees must be properly trained.
Only approved authentication mechanisms must be utilized by the contracting party.

When users are provided with new or updated secret authentication information, they must get temporary credentials, which must be changed upon first use. The secret authentication information must be valid for no longer than 24 hours.

Legal entity’s authentication information must not be used for non-business purposes. This includes but is not limited to not using the same password for the legal entity used and privately used user accounts.
Secret authentication information must be changed when suspected of compromise.
Passwords and PINs must be defined, kept safe and managed securely.
Login-credentials must consider the following:
Secret authentication information such as passwords, PINs, keys and tokens must be classified as strictly confidential and protected by cryptographic measures.
Passwords must not be displayed by default as clear characters on the screen when being entered but must be hidden.
Where possible, legal entity owned ICT Systems should leverage central identity provider services, which manage the user passwords.
User passwords (including technical accounts) must not be stored in ICT Systems in plaintext format, should be suitably protected and stored separately from ICT System data.
User passwords must be protected by encryption during their transmission.
Password transmission must be justified and authorized.
Only authorized individuals and components must be allowed to trigger the change of passwords.
A password management policy must be enforced with at least the following criteria:
Passwords for primary access must be at least 14 characters long with a lifelong validity.
Passwords for non-privileged secondary access must be at least 14 characters long with a lifelong validity.
Passwords for privileged access must be changed at least every 90 days.
If 14 characters are technically not feasible, passwords must be at least 8 characters long and must be changed at least every 90 days.
New passwords must be different from at least the last 6 passwords.

Initial account passwords must be set up by Account Owners, latest during the first login to the ICT System. Alternatively, users might be given a temporary password by the ICT System administrator that must be changed during first login. This temporary password must be valid for no longer than 24 hours.
Password reset or recovery processes must follow the same rules as the initial password setup. Additionally, the identity of the requestor must be verified by the Asset Owner.
All default ICT System accounts must be removed, disabled, or have their default passwords changed.
A password must at least contain characters of each of the following categories: upper case characters, lower case characters, numbers, special characters.
Every password change / reset must be logged and forwarded to SIEM.
PINs must be at least 4 digits long and have a lifelong validity. Following a risk-based approach, the minimum number of digits must be increased.

Policies and protocols for strong authentication mechanisms must be designed, implemented and controlled based on results of the data classification and the outcome of the ICT risk assessment processes (e.g., cryptographic measures must be commensurate to the classification of the data).
Any credentialing concept that utilizes other means then passwords, such as passphrases, must provide bit entropy at least on the same level as the current password policy.
Secure authentication mechanisms must be defined, developed, and applied.
All legal entity owned ICT Systems must allow access to their resources only after users have been successfully authenticated and authorized.
Confidential data must be accessible only if the user is authenticated with a strong two- or multi-factor authentication.
Where possible, ICT Systems should leverage Single-Sign-On (SSO) features provided centrally.
If user credentials input is required, the log-on process must follow the following criteria:
Log-on information must be validated only upon completion of all input data.
Authentication information, such as credentials, is only evaluated on the target ICT System, not on the client device.
Brute-force protection must be implemented. The account must be locked after a maximum of 10 unsuccessful log-on attempts.
When log-on fails, the error message must not provide any information to the user on the root cause of log-on failure.
Depending on the criticality of confidentiality and authenticity protection goal and exposure of the IT Application, the IT Application must use dedicated robust authentication schemes.
For multi-factor authentication, only standard legal entity approved solutions must be used as the second and additional factors.
Two- or multi-factor authentication must be enforced, independent from legal entity’s endpoints.
Locked accounts can only be released after secure user identity validation.
Unlock of locked accounts must be justified, authorized, and documented.
Any successful / unsuccessful log-on attempts must be logged.
Authentication methods must be applied according to the established classification for Identity and Access Management and the overall risk profile of IT Assets.

Strong authentication methods must be established for remote access, for privileged access, for access to IT Assets supporting critical or important functions or for IT Assets that are publicly accessible.

A risk-based authentication concept for web-based IT Applications and those capable of handling federation protocol-based tokens must be implemented. The authentication strength must be in line with the Segregation Area and the application protection needs.
Primary and secondary accesses must be defined, assigned, documented, managed, and controlled.
The primary and secondary access to legal entities’ ICT Systems must be activated or de-activated based on the information provided by HR and/or Third-Party Management.

Removal or adjustment of access must be processed timely in the target ICT System. If this cannot be done automatically, complementary controls must be in place to ensure near-time processing: ‘Near-time’ should be determined as 1 working day for publicly-accessible-applications that have at least one protection goal classified critical, and 3 working days for all other applications.
Inactive primary access accounts must be identified and deactivated after an inactivity period of 30 days.

Based on HR’s information about individuals leaving the company, primary access must be revoked on the first day after the leaver date, secondary access, and all access rights within three working days, all accounts must be removed as soon as possible – latest within 42 days.

In case a user moves within the organization, all existing access related to the user must be recertified by the new line manager within two weeks. This includes only secondary access that was explicitly requested and not primary access.
Shared and non-personal accounts must be defined, assigned, documented, managed, and controlled to prevent any unauthorized access or breach of access controls.
Non-personal accounts and shared user accounts must be limited, inventoried and the traceability to responsible persons must be ensured.
Each shared account is assigned to an Account Owner, who is responsible for maintaining an inventory of all individuals that have access to the shared accounts.
Login-credentials of shared / non-personal accounts as well as all secret authentications must be securely created, stored in a vault and handled.
Login-credentials for shared user IDs remaining active should be changed upon termination or change of employment, contract, or agreement.
In case identity / personal account is decommissioned, ownership of corresponding shared accounts must be reviewed and updated, if necessary.
Interactive shared accounts must be traceable for all actions to an individual person and limited to actions by one individual at any given time.
Privileged accounts (PAM) must be defined, assigned, documented, managed, monitored and controlled to avoid unauthorized usage and harm to IT Assets.

Privileged, emergency and administration access rights must be assigned on a need-to-use or ad-hoc basis for all ICT Systems. Where feasible, for administration, dedicated accounts must be used and automated privileged access management procedures must be implemented.
The interactive use of privileged built-in accounts must be prevented and if applicable, the entitlements of these accounts must be transferred to dedicated user IDs.
Privileged access must always be marked as such in Authorization Concept.
Privileged access must be classified and controlled according to their level of criticality on a risk-based approach.
Privileged built-in accounts must be classified and documented in the Authorization Concept.
All privileged accounts must be inventoried in a privileged account inventory.
Onboarded and managed in PAM: Privileged accounts must be secured in the vault of a Privileged Access Management (PAM) solution.
Completeness, currentness, and accuracy of the privileged account inventory must be ensured.
Measures and criteria to manage and handle privileged accounts must be defined, implemented, monitored and controlled to avoid unauthorized usage and harm to IT Assets.
Idle Session Timeout: The use of privileged access must be time-limited based on their level of criticality.

Separate privileged from non-privileged account: Dedicated user IDs must be created and used for privileged access. Dedicated user IDs must be marked and identifiable for privileged access. Privileged access must not be assigned to user IDs with regular business / IT roles and must be provided based on the function using the least privilege principle.
Release of locked privileged accounts must be detected and justified.

Privileged accounts must be monitored and logged. The details must be made available to the Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) for analysis and detection of unauthorized privileged accesses.
Logging and Monitoring: Logs must be made available for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) in a structured way to allow the detection of unauthorized privileged accesses.
Access to privileged accounts must be technically enforced to require a valid approved change request, ICT incident ticket, or a reference to a catalog of recurring routine activities.
Video Session Recording / Text / Key stroke Logging: Any interactive use of privileged accounts by individuals must be recorded through the PAM solution and regularly reviewed on a risk basis.

Credentials Obfuscation (Disable Password View / Copy): The passwords for privileged accounts must remain hidden and must not be subject to copying. De-obfuscation for Emergency Accounts and Break Glass Accounts is allowed, provided that: all other Privileged Access Management (PAM) control requirements in ID: 11, 12 and 13 are implemented (including traceability to individuals); passwords must be automatically rotated after being retrieved from the secure storage and utilized; any use of emergency access must be documented, and a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) alert must be sent in the event of account usage.
The recertification of access rights and role compositions must be defined, integrated in the access procedure, monitored and controlled.
The following types of recertification must be performed and documented:
User access recertification must take place every 6 months for business-critical access and for privileged access of all levels by the responsible Line Manager and respective Role Owners.
User access recertification must take place every 12 months for all other accesses by the responsible Line Manager.

The following types of recertification must be performed and documented: Role composition recertification by the Role Owner and Asset Owner must take place every 12 months and must include birth right roles.
All unauthorized access, which has been identified during the recertification process, must be revoked after the recertifier’s sign-off.
Dedicated access to legal entity data must be reviewed at least once every 12 months by an employee of the respective legal entity.
Tier-0 access must be managed, secured and kept safe.
Tier-0 access must additionally comply with the following control requirements:
Threat Analytics SIEM / PAM: Session monitoring solution must allow for data analysis / logging of actions made by privileged access.
Maximum Session Time / Time-limited Access: Use of privileged access must be time-limited to the necessary minimum.

In emergency situations, the approval for privileged access must occur through the responsible Manager on Duty. The Ticket Owner must ensure that the ICT incident documentation including approval is provided within 24 hours.
A procedure for Cloud Identity Access Management must be defined, implemented, monitored and controlled to protect against unauthorized usage or privilege escalation of Cloud-related accounts.
Federated identities should be used, controlled, and traceability of access must be ensured.
Federated identities must be technically linked to a valid MyUserID or Account Owner Workgroup.
Access event logs to IT Assets must be available and monitored.
CSP must only be able to access legal entity data and ICT Systems in the cloud after prior and explicit approval for each individual case.
Access requests by CSPs personnel to legal entity’s data must go through an access request process that requires explicit approval by the respective information owner.
The CSP must only be able to use “just in time” (temporary) credentials when technically feasible rather than persistent credentials based on the service models.
Access to cloud environments must be restricted and, where possible, only via the programmatic call of APIs ("infrastructure-as-code").
Cloud assets must use accounts which are centrally managed by the IAM process.
It must be ensured that networks are designed in line with the established IT security requirements.
Relevant established requirements as well as best practices or standards within the industry must be taken into account when designing networks.
The network architecture and the network security design must be reviewed annually to identify potential vulnerabilities.

The network topologies with all network connections and data flows must be documented, including but not limited to the clear specification of relevant elements like network security zones, network segments and their classification based on the assigned IT applications in the respective segment.
The documentation on network topology must be reviewed and updated after major network changes or at least annually.

Architecture guidance and best practices for the use of cloud services must be established to get the right balance between usage of cloud native services and avoidance of lock-in by providing the required interoperability and portability where needed.
It must be ensured through appropriate network configuration that all network and infrastructure components are securely configured and hardened.

Secure configuration and hardening baselines for all network and infrastructure components must be defined, documented, implemented and, for components in the Red and Yellow Segregation Areas regularly be reviewed in line with the ICT Operations Guideline.
All instructions from vendors as well as best practices and standards within the industry, that can serve as a robust benchmark, must be followed.
Hardening baselines must be implemented and verified before using a new or changed infrastructure component in the Red Segregation Area in line with the ICT Operations Guideline.
Procedures must be in place to limit, lock and terminate ICT systems and remote sessions after a specific period of inactivity.
Configuration files of security-relevant network components must be secured against tampering (running configuration files and start-up configuration files).
It must be ensured that network services are managed, and security features are documented in a way that ensures consistent and secure service delivery.

A regular process must be defined and implemented to identify, specify, document, and monitor IT and information security measures and features (typically in a service catalogue, or Asset Security Documentation (ASD)), service levels and management requirements of all network services with their defined scope and applicability.
It must be specified whether the services are provided by an ICT third-party service provider or an internal service provider.

A regular process for managing network services must be defined as part of the network operational documentation and include responsibilities, standard and emergency operation procedures, defined implementation rules and related communication as part of change management process.
The scope of documentation must be in accordance with the asset specifications documented in an asset inventory.
Each network segment must have a defined list of allowed access protocols.

It must be ensured that access to network-connected IT Assets, especially networks and network services, are controlled through stringent access controls and authentication mechanisms to ensure only authorized entities can connect and access the resources.
Secure access to IT Assets from devices used for remote work must be ensured.

Network access controls must be identified and implemented to prevent and detect network connections by unauthorized devices or ICT systems, including endpoints not meeting the defined security requirements.
The network connection between external and internal ICT Systems must only be established after authentication and must be encrypted.
All IT Assets connecting to the corporate network of the legal entity’s internal wireless infrastructure must be authenticated.
Access to internal legal entity ICT systems and networks from external/non-legal entity networks must only be possible after two-factor-authentication via approved legal entity environments.
All ICT Systems, including IT Applications, and users must only have access to networks and network services that they have been specifically authorized to use based on the need-to-know principle.

control_description: Protection of network connections and data in transit
control_requirement: Network connections, including data in transit, must be protected in a way that preserves their integrity and ensures confidentiality.

control_description: Protection of network connections and data in transit
control_requirement: Network connections, with the respective communication protocols used, as well as data in transit passing over all types of networks must be encrypted to preserve confidentiality, integrity, availability, and authenticity in line with the Encryption and Key Management Guideline by using standardized, secure cryptographic protocols (e.g., TLS) with legal entity approved cryptographic measures and a secure configuration to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. The following must be ensured:

control_description: Protection of network connections and data in transit
control_requirement: Procedures must be established to assess compliance with the requirements on the protection of data during network transmission.

control_description: Protection of network connections and data in transit
control_requirement: Network traffic between internal networks and the Internet as well as other external connections must be secured.
Dedicated environments must be provided in accordance with their intended use.
Red, Yellow, Blue and Green segregation areas must be segregated at least logically.
A physically separate network test lab must be provided for testing and acceptance testing of on-premises network services.
It must be ensured that networks are segregated appropriately.
Groups of network connected IT Assets must be segmented and segregated into different types of network security zones according to their purpose:
The network security zones types must at least be logically segregated from each other.
Within the network security zone types the network-connected IT Assets must be segregated on a risk-based approach.
Within the Internet and Partner network security zone types, the network-connected IT Assets must be assigned to their own DMZ on a risk-based approach.

The following must be considered in the risk-based approach for segregation: The criticality or importance of the function those ICT Systems, including networks, support The established classification The overall risk profile of IT Assets using those ICT Systems, including networks
All network-connected IT Assets must be assigned to a network security zone that corresponds to their use case.
The perimeter of each network security zone must be defined.
Connections from external networks must be terminated in designated DMZ and must be protected by two-stage firewall (inner and outer) which are from different vendors.
For SaaS, equivalent protection level should be applied.

For IaaS and PaaS where network controls are harmonized with internal networks, PaaS and IaaS can be treated as internal networks. Otherwise, the same protections for external networks must be applied.

If a DMZ is not used, whether due to business model limitations or other valid reasons, a justification must be documented and an equivalent solutions with an adequate verified level of protection must be implemented.
For the administration of IT Assets, a separate and dedicated network must be used.

Automated mechanisms must be in place and the network connection infrastructure must be designed in a way that allows to temporarily isolate, where necessary, subnetworks, network components and network connected IT Assets instantaneously.
Firewalls and connection filters must be implemented and managed to ensure reliable and strict control of data traffic between networks on an ongoing basis.
Firewall configurations must prevent any unauthorized connections between network security zones.
Firewall rules must be implemented according to defined criteria for network connectivity.
Implementation and removal of firewall rules must follow defined procedures, if possible, with an automatic workflow.
If provisioning is done manually, additional controls (four-eyes-principle) must be established.
Roles, responsibilities and steps for the specification, implementation, approval, change and review of firewall rules and connection filters must be identified in defined procedures.
Firewall rules and connection filters must be recertified regularly and adhere to all of the following:
The recertification must be performed in accordance with the established classification and the overall risk profile of ICT Systems involved.
For ICT Systems supporting critical or important functions, the adequacy of existing firewall rules and connection filters must be recertified at least every 6 months.
All requests - including the justification for the firewall rule - must be documented (to ensure traceability).
Deviations from the Network Adequacy Matrix must be approved.
Web-application firewalls must be installed in front of internet-facing web-based applications.
The desktop firewall and/or application firewall must ensure that only authorized traffic enters or leaves the ICT System.
It must be ensured that perimeters are secured in such a way that unauthorized access and connections are prevented.
Protective mechanisms must be implemented at each network security zone transition.
Only necessary and allowed connectivity (according to applicable Security Documentation (SD) /Network Adequacy Matrix) between network security zones must be implemented.
All inbound and outbound network traffic must be controlled, monitored based on the confidentiality class of the IT Assets, and denied by default by the principle of explicit allowance.
IDS and IPS must be in place to analyze all network traffic between network security zones to ensure that attacks or misuse are actively prevented.
IDS and IPS must be updated at defined intervals on a risk-based approach.

Risk-based technical security measures must be implemented that are capable of detecting and responding to network-based attacks based on anomalous input or output traffic patterns and/or distributed denial of service (DDoS) and denial of service (DoS), including corresponding filtering capabilities.
When using cloud services, the CSP must allow for controls to minimize and protect the perimeter of Publicly Accessible Endpoints.
It must be ensured that no network traffic could bypass perimeter security (e.g. firewalls, SDN). The protection used at the perimeter must be stateful.
It must be ensured that suitable web filtering is in place to prevent access to unauthorized or insecure resources.

Proxies must check all unencrypted and encrypted communications. To do this, for all encrypted connections between external and internal networks, interception and inspection must be possible at the proxy, in both directions.
The management of blacklisted (denied) or whitelisted (allowed) destinations on proxies must be defined.
Proxies must be able to protect from prohibited targets, detect malware and protect users and ICT systems from malicious content.
Bypassing the proxies must be prevented by appropriate configuration.
All proxy rules, including exceptions (whitelisting), must be revalidated at defined intervals.

Access to external websites must be managed based on defined processes for website white- and blacklisting, covering the following aspects: Roles and responsibilities Baseline of proxy rules Management of exceptional approvals process Management of proxy rule recertifications at defined intervals Monitoring activities

Access to the following types of websites must be blocked: Known or suspected malicious websites Command and control servers Malicious websites acquired from threat intelligence Websites sharing illegal content
